content: The role of a poisons information specialist involves responding to telephone inquiries regarding poisoning incidents. This requires specialized training tailored to the needs of the poisons information center and its users. To ensure uniformity in staff expertise, each center should develop a comprehensive training program that aligns with local circumstances. Typically, the training period lasts about three months, though this may vary depending on the center's resources and staff skills. The objectives of the training program are to ensure that new poisons information specialists: Understand their responsibilities and role within the poisons center team. Are confident in the operational procedures of the poisons center. Are competent in handling telephone inquiries about poisoning cases. Can efficiently locate the necessary information to address inquiries. Recognize when to escalate inquiries to senior colleagues if the case exceeds their expertise. Possess knowledge of the toxicology of commonly encountered poisons. Are familiar with the basic principles of managing poisoned patients. A robust training program should include presentations on both common and rare poisoning agents, clinical scenarios, directed reading, and practical experience in telephone communication and triage. These skills are critical for effective handling of inquiries. Training methods are further detailed in the WHO poisons center training manual. After completing the training, trainees must demonstrate their competence through assessments before they are allowed to handle calls independently. In addition to initial training, all staff should engage in ongoing professional development to stay updated on the latest practices in poisoning management. This can include in-house case discussions, journal clubs, meetings with other poisons centers, attendance at international conferences, and other forms of continuing education. The training program for new staff should cover the following areas: 1. Local Policies and Procedures: Trainees should be introduced to the center's operating procedures, including how to handle inquiries from specific groups such as the police, media, or legal teams. They should also learn escalation protocols for cases requiring senior input or those with broader implications, such as chemical incidents or deliberate toxic substance releases. 2. Principles of Clinical Toxicology: Trainees should gain an understanding of human physiology, pharmacology, routes of exposure, mechanisms of toxicity, recognition of toxidromes, and general management principles, including decontamination, symptomatic care, antidotes, and elimination enhancement methods. 3. Assessment of Poisoned Patients: Trainees should learn to interpret physiological parameters, identify red flags indicating severe toxicity, and understand the basics of electrocardiography and blood gas analysis in poisoning cases. 4. Subject Knowledge: Training should focus on the toxicology and management of common poisons encountered in the region, as well as less common but highly toxic substances. Directed reading and clinical scenarios should supplement teaching sessions to reinforce knowledge and identify gaps. 5. Information Sources: Trainees should become familiar with the center's information resources, including internal documents, scientific journals, databases, and external consultants. They should also learn to identify the most appropriate sources for specific inquiries and understand backup arrangements in case of technical failures. 6. Telephone Service and Communication Skills: Effective communication is essential for handling inquiries. Trainees should develop skills in questioning callers, taking accurate histories, active listening, showing empathy, and managing difficult conversations. Experiential learning under supervision is the most effective way to build these skills. Trainees should also learn to handle specific scenarios, such as suicidal callers, therapeutic errors, and media inquiries. 7. Documentation: Accurate and consistent documentation of poisoning cases is critical for medico-legal purposes, research, toxicovigilance, and statistical analysis. Trainees should be trained to complete inquiry records clearly, scientifically, and promptly, understanding the importance of thorough documentation. 8. Assessment and Examination: After completing the training program, trainees should undergo formal assessments to ensure they meet the required competence levels. This may include examinations, checklists, or supervised call thresholds. Once certified as competent, trainees can handle inquiries independently and join the staff rotation. For medical toxicologists, who are physicians specializing in the management of poisoned patients, training involves both didactic and practical components. This includes clinical experience in diagnosing and treating poisoning cases, as well as understanding toxicodynamics, toxicokinetics, and the management of various poisoning scenarios. Training programs for medical toxicologists vary by country and may include fellowships or placements in clinical toxicology units.
